title: The Umayyad Mosque
hook: the great mosque of Damascus, built on a site holy for centuries, still has a shrine honoring Yahya (John the Baptist)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Dome of the Rock: a bare rock in Jerusalem, an octagon raised around it, and the night journey remembered there. Your line was: a dome over the rock. What did you choose to build around rather than over? Day nine hundred five.

In the prayer hall of the great mosque of Damascus, among the rows of carpet and the columns, stands a small domed shrine behind a grille. People stop at it. Some touch the grille. Some pray beside it. Christians come to it too. It honors a prophet the Qur'an calls Yahya, and Christians call John the Baptist. Tradition says his head is buried there. A shrine to John inside a mosque, in the old capital of the caliphs. Today: the Umayyad Mosque.

Start with the ground under it. The histories describe this site as holy before Islam: a temple in Roman times, and later a church dedicated to John the Baptist. Later histories report that after the Muslims came to Damascus, for a time Muslims and Christians both prayed on the site. Then the Umayyad caliph al-Walid, son of Abd al-Malik, built the great mosque here, reusing the old walls. So the mosque stands on layer upon layer of prayer. And it kept John. The Qur'an tells Yahya's story with warmth. Of him it says: "Peace on him the day he was born, and the day he dieth and the day he shall be raised alive!" A prophet greeted with peace at birth, at death and on the day of rising. There is another layer, looking forward. One of the mosque's minarets is called the Minaret of Jesus. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that Jesus son of Mary will descend near a white minaret east of Damascus, and tradition links that report to this tower. So one building holds a Roman past, a Christian past, a Muslim present, and a hope about the end of days. Then there is the courtyard, wide and open, and the gold mosaics of trees and rivers and houses on the walls, which some readers see as a picture of paradise. Old stone, many prayers, one place. Layers of holiness.

The practice: pray for Damascus. Settle, and breathe. Bring the courtyard to mind: wide stone, open sky, pigeons, minarets above. Then think of the city around it, a very old city, home to families of more than one faith, a city that has lived through hard years. If you pray, you can ask God for peace on Damascus and its people, in your own words or in silence. If you don't, hold the city in mind with goodwill, one breath at a time. The bell holds the time.
The Umayyad Mosque. The great mosque of Damascus, built on a site of older prayer, with a shrine to Yahya, John the Baptist, inside it. Today's word.
Your line: layers of holiness. Today, in a familiar place, ask who prayed, worked or lived there before you. Give them a moment's thanks. Day nine hundred five.

howItsDone: Worshipers at the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus pray in its great hall and visit the shrine honoring Yahya (John the Baptist), which Christian visitors also come to.

original.note: Arabic: Yahya, the Qur'an's name for John the Baptist.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Umayyad Mosque is simply a big old mosque.
what it means: it stands on a temple and a church, keeps a shrine to John the Baptist, and has a minaret named for Jesus.
what a scholar hears: the reports in al-Baladhuri of Muslims and Christians sharing the site before al-Walid's building, and the hadith of al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an on the white minaret east of Damascus.

al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan (the church of John in Damascus, the shared site, al-Walid's mosque)

notes: Sahih Muslim 2937 paraphrased; confirm the number and that the link to the mosque's Minaret of Jesus is presented as tradition.
The Roman temple, the church of John, and the period of shared use are reported by historians; confirm the framing ('the historians report').
'Tradition says his head is buried there' kept as tradition.
'Some readers see the mosaics as a picture of paradise' is attributed to some readers, not stated as fact.
The practice mentions Damascus having 'lived through hard years' without naming events; check tone.
'Christians come to it too' is a general description of visitors; confirm.
Index hook says 'holy for centuries'; the teaser keeps the index line, the voice avoids the count.
Editor: the Roman temple and church are now attributed to the histories rather than stated flatly; cut the narrator's verdict 'it is fitting'.

Audit (2026-10-01): the shared-prayer period is now attributed to 'later histories' (it rests on later reports); removed 'tradition says' from al-Walid's building, which is well documented; cut a line repeating the hook's shrine.
